01 · Why measuring is hard · what good means
Good = quality AND variety
Quality (fidelity): each image looks real, sharp, no glitches.
Variety (diversity): the images cover all of the training data.
Match: fakes as a group follow the real distribution.
GAN draws…
quality
variety

Why we need both: a score that checks only one of them can be fooled by the other failure.
Unit 3 · 5 / 77
01 · Why measuring is hard · bad idea 1
Bad idea 1: just look
Show a grid of samples. Say “looks good”.
Subjective: different people disagree.
Not scalable: no one can compare 50 models by eye.
Cherry-picking: show the best samples, hide the bad ones.
Blind to collapse: a 16-image grid can’t show that only 3 of 100 modes exist.
Why we need a number: our eyes can’t be repeated, scaled or trusted to count modes.
Unit 3 · 6 / 77
01 · Why measuring is hard · bad idea 2
Bad idea 2: read D’s loss
1
At balance D says 0.5 for every image, real or fake.
2
BCE loss = −ln 0.5 − ln(1 − 0.5) = 0.693 + 0.693 = 2 ln 2 ≈ 1.386
D’s loss sits near 1.386 for good and bad images.
A low D loss may only mean D is bad at its job.
The W-loss from Unit 2 tracks progress better. It is still not a quality score.
Why we need an outside judge: D’s loss measures the contest, not the images.

01 · Why measuring is hard · the wish list
What a good metric needs
1
Sees images through a trained network (features, not pixels).
2
Measures quality and variety together.
3
Compares fakes with real images.
4
Gives one number per model.
5
Has a clear direction: lower (or higher) = better.
Why we need this list: we will grade IS and FID against it.

01 · Why measuring is hard · check
Check: why measuring is hard
1
Why can’t we report accuracy for a GAN?
There is no correct answer: a new face is not right or wrong.
2
G draws one perfect face again and again. Which goal fails?
Variety: high quality, zero variety (mode collapse).
3
D’s BCE loss is 1.386. Are the images good?
Can’t tell: 2 ln 2 ≈ 1.386 is the balance value for good and bad images.
Why it matters: each answer points to one wish on our list.

02 · Inception Score · all images
All images: one class, or spread?
Every image → “dog”
Low variety.
This is mode collapse.
Spread across classes
Dog, cat, car, boat, plane…
High variety.
p(y|x) = one image’s probabilities. Want: peaked (quality).
p(y) = average of p(y|x) over all images. Want: spread out (variety).
Why we need both views: one image shows quality; all images together show variety.
Unit 3 · 13 / 77
02 · Inception Score · the formula
The IS formula, read aloud
IS = exp( Ex [ KL( p(y|x) ‖ p(y) ) ] )
KL( p(y|x) ‖ p(y) ): how different one image’s guess is from the overall guess. KL is the gap measure from Unit 2.
Ex[ … ]: average that gap over all images.
exp( … ): turn the average into the final score.
High when each image is sharp AND the images disagree.
Why we need the KL: it is big only when quality and variety are both high.
Unit 3 · 14 / 77
02 · Inception Score · worked example
IS with 3 classes, by hand
Given: 3 classes, 3 images. Image 1 puts 0.9 on class 1, image 2 on class 2, image 3 on class 3; 0.05 on each other class. p(y) = average = (1/3, 1/3, 1/3)
1
Big term: 0.9 × ln(0.9 ÷ 1/3) = 0.9 × 0.993 = 0.894
2
Two small terms: 2 × 0.05 × ln(0.05 ÷ 1/3) = 0.1 × (−1.897) = −0.190
3
KL = 0.894 − 0.190 = 0.704 (the same for every image)
4
IS = exp(0.704) = 2.02 (max with 3 classes = 3)
5
Collapse: all images = class 1 → p(y) = p(y|x) → KL = 0 → IS = 1
Why we need the hand calculation: it shows IS rewarding sharp, different guesses and falling to 1 on collapse.

Never looks at real data

03 · FID · two clouds
Two clouds of points
good GAN
bad GAN
clouds overlap → low FID
shifted, wider → high FID
○ real · ● fake · + = centre (μ) · 2-D sketch of 2,048-D
Each image = one point in feature space.
Centre of a cloud = mean μ.
Spread and shape of a cloud = covariance Σ.
FID compares μ and Σ of the real and fake clouds.
Why we need μ and Σ: they shrink thousands of points into two summaries we can compare.
Unit 3 · 21 / 77
03 · FID · the formula
The FID formula in two parts
FID = ‖μr − μf‖² + Tr( Σr + Σf − 2√(Σr Σf) )
r = real, f = fake
Part 1: ‖μr − μf‖² Are the centres close?
Part 2: Tr( … ) Are the spreads and shapes alike?
Don’t memorise it. Know the two parts.
FID = squared Wasserstein-2 distance between two Gaussians. A cousin of Unit 2’s W.
Why we need two parts: a fake cloud can be off-centre, the wrong shape, or both.
Unit 3 · 22 / 77
03 · FID · worked example
FID in 1-D, by hand
Given (one feature only): real: μr = 0, σr = 1 · fake: μf = 0.5, σf = 2 In 1-D, Σ is just σ²: Σr = 1, Σf = 4
1
Mean part: (μr − μf)² = (0 − 0.5)² = 0.25
2
Spread part: 1 + 4 − 2 × √(1 × 4) = 5 − 4 = 1
3
Check: (σr − σf)² = (1 − 2)² = 1 ✓
4
FID = mean part 0.25 + spread part 1 = 1.25
The wrong spread (1) costs more than the shifted centre (0.25).
Why we need the spread part: a GAN with the right centre but the wrong variety still pays.

04 · FID in practice · the pipeline
FID in five steps
Story so far: We know what FID measures. Now: computing it correctly.
real + fake
10,000–50,000 each
Inception v3
pool3 layer
2,048 numbers
per image
mean + covariance
per set
FID
one number
1
Collect 10,000–50,000 real images from the training set.
2
Generate the same number of fakes from G.
3
Run every image through Inception → 2,048 numbers each.
4
Per set: a mean (2,048 numbers) and a covariance (2,048 × 2,048).
5
Put the two means and two covariances into the FID formula.
Why we need the five steps: skip or change one and the FID number is wrong.
Unit 3 · 26 / 77
04 · FID in practice · preparing images
Getting MNIST ready for Inception
Inception expects colour photos, 3 × 299 × 299. Our G makes 1 × 28 × 28 grey digits in [−1, 1].
1
Scale [−1, 1] to [0, 1]: (x + 1) ÷ 2, so −1 → 0 and 1 → 1.
2
Repeat the grey sheet 3 times → 3 × 28 × 28 (R = G = B).
3
Resize to 3 × 299 × 299, Inception’s input size.
4
ImageNet normalisation: subtract mean (0.485, 0.456, 0.406), divide by std (0.229, 0.224, 0.225).
The same four steps for real images and for fakes.
Why we need this preparation: Inception only gives useful features for the input it was trained on.

Unit 3 · 30 / 77
04 · FID in practice · preparation
Same preparation for both sides
✗ Bad
Real images: bilinear resize.
Fakes: nearest-neighbour resize.
FID can move by 5–10 points.
✓ Good
Same resize method for both.
Same normalisation for both.
Same everything else.
A different resize alone changes the number, not the GAN.
Different Inception weights give FIDs not comparable with papers.
Use a standard FID implementation with the original weights (e.g. Clean-FID).
Why we need identical preparation: FID should measure the GAN, not the resizing.

Unit 3 · 33 / 77
04 · FID in practice · a warning
FID = 0 is suspicious
FID = 0 → the two feature clouds are identical; three possible causes:
1
G truly learned the data
Possible, but very unlikely.
2
G memorised
It copies training images.
Overfitting, not generating.
3
Real vs real
You fed real images in as the “fakes” by mistake.
Check for memorising: for each fake, find its nearest training image. Near-copies mean G memorised.
Why we need this check: a perfect score can hide a copying machine or a bug.
Unit 3 · 34 / 77
04 · FID in practice · limits
What FID cannot tell you
Assumes Gaussian features: real ones are not exactly Gaussian.
Biased at small N: too few images push FID up.
Misses fine detail: small quality differences barely move it.
Only as good as Inception: far from ImageNet photos, its features mean less.
Says THAT images are bad, not WHY.
Why we need to know the limits: one number never tells the whole story.

05 · Beyond one number · two scores
Precision and recall
Precision = quality
Of all fakes, what share look real?
Recall = variety
Of all real kinds, what share can G produce?
GAN B: sharp digits → high precision.
GAN A: blurry digits → low precision.
GAN B: 6 of 10 digits → low recall.
GAN A: all 10 digits → high recall.
Why we need two scores: quality and variety are measured apart, not mixed.

Unit 3 · 39 / 77
05 · Beyond one number · quick check
Check: measuring GANs
1
A rival reports FID 20 on 1,000 images; you get 30 on 50,000 — who is better?
Unknown, maybe the rival: small N pushes FID up, so their 20 is already inflated.
2
Why does IS not notice a GAN that draws perfect dogs from a cat dataset?
IS never looks at real images.
3
In 1-D, which costs more FID: shift the mean by 0.5, or double σ from 1 to 2?
Shift: 0.5² = 0.25. Double σ: (2 − 1)² = 1.0 → doubling σ costs more.
Why it matters: a metric is only useful if you know how it can mislead.

06 · Strengths and weaknesses · strengths
What GANs do well
Story so far: We can now score a GAN. Now: where do GANs win and lose against other generators?
Sharp images
D punishes blur.
So G learns crisp detail.
Fast sampling
One pass through G = one image.
Good for real-time apps.
Smooth latent space
Walk in z to morph images.
Steer features (Unit 2).
Flexible idea
An adversarial loss can be added to other models.
Pix2Pix and CycleGAN do this (Units 4–5).
Why we need this list: it tells us when a GAN is the right tool.
Unit 3 · 41 / 77
06 · Strengths and weaknesses · weaknesses
Where GANs struggle
1
Unstable training: two players can swing instead of settling.
2
Mode collapse: G may cover only part of the data (low recall).
3
No likelihood: a GAN cannot say how probable an image is, p(x).
4
Hard to evaluate: we needed IS, FID, precision and recall.
5
Hard to invert: no built-in way to go from an image back to its z.
Why we need this list: Units 1–3 fixed 1, 2 and 4; 3 and 5 stay GAN limits.

07 · Bias and fairness · what is bias?
A good FID can still be unfair
Story so far: We can now measure a GAN. Now: what if a ‘good’ GAN learned the wrong things?
Bias in a GAN
The outputs don’t fairly show the diversity of the real world, or even of the training data.
Faces: almost only light-skinned.
Faces: mostly young.
Digits: one writing style ignored.
Why we need to check for bias: sharp images with a low FID can still leave people out.
Unit 3 · 44 / 77
07 · Bias and fairness · three levels
Three places bias enters
1
Data bias
The training data is unbalanced.
80% light skin, 20% dark skin.
2
Model bias
The GAN amplifies it.
80 / 20 drifts toward e.g. 95 / 5.
reported for face GANs, Jain et al. 2020
3
Evaluation bias
FID says “good”.
The majority looks great; the minority is averaged away.
Why we need all three levels: fixing only one still lets bias in through the others.

07 · Bias and fairness · mode collapse
Mode collapse is a fairness problem
Faces
50 face types in the data.
After collapse: only 5 survive.
Survivors: the majority groups.
Lost: mostly the minority groups.
MNIST (about 6,000 of each digit)

Survive: the “easy” 1, 0, 7.
Collapse: the “hard” 8, 9, 4.
Not random: which modes die follows a pattern.
Why we need to treat collapse as bias: it erases the groups that were already rare.
Unit 3 · 48 / 77
07 · Bias and fairness · real harms
Real harms
Synthetic training data
GAN makes mostly light-skinned faces. → a face detector trained on them works worse on dark skin.
Medical augmentation
Synthetic X-rays learned from one hospital’s patients. → the model works worse on other populations.
Creative tools
Trained mostly on Western art. → other cultural styles shown poorly or stereotyped.
Deepfake detection
Detectors trained on biased fakes. → worse at catching fakes of minority faces.
Why we need to care: biased GAN images become biased training data for other systems.

07 · Bias and fairness · reducing bias
Five ways to reduce bias
way
how
note
1 Balance the data
repeat old faces or use fewer young ones
repeats can overfit; dropping wastes data
2 Conditional GAN
each group its own label → its own signal
quality gaps may remain
3 Loss weighting
80/20 data: young weight 0.2, old 0.8
D and G focus more on the 20% group
4 Per-group evaluation
an FID for every group
finds gaps, does not fix them
5 Diverse data
collect, audit, document limits
slow, but the best fix
No algorithm fully fixes biased data: prevention is best.
Why we need several fixes: each one covers a different level of bias.
Unit 3 · 52 / 77
07 · Bias and fairness · the tension
Fair can mean a higher FID
Fairness checks
Per-group FID: similar for every group
Demographic parity: each group made equally often
Quality parity: each group equally realistic
Coverage: all subgroups appear (age × ethnicity × style)
1
Real data: 80 / 20.
2
A GAN that copies 80 / 20, bias included → low FID.
3
Rebalance to 50 / 50: fakes no longer match the data → FID goes UP.
FID rewards copying the data, biases and all. A fair GAN may score a higher FID, and that is acceptable.
Why we need fairness metrics: FID alone would push us back toward the biased GAN.

Why we need a checklist: bias is easy to miss unless you ask on purpose.

Unit 3 · 57 / 77
08 · StyleGAN · W-space
Why W untangles features
Z-space: what we sample
Drawn from N(0, 1).
It must fill a round bell shape. So features are forced to mix to fit it.
W-space: what G uses
Made by the mapping network.
No shape rule. It can stretch to the data’s shape. So features can separate.
The mapping network learns the bend from the round Z to the data-shaped W.
Why we need W: in W, one direction can mean one feature.
Unit 3 · 58 / 77
08 · StyleGAN · recap
Recap: instance normalisation
Instance norm: per channel, per image → mean 0, std 1. Given: one channel of one image holds 2, 4, 6, 8.
1
Mean = (2 + 4 + 6 + 8) ÷ 4 = 5
2
Squared gaps from 5: 9, 1, 1, 9 → average 20 ÷ 4 = 5 → std = √5 ≈ 2.24
3
x_norm = (x − 5) ÷ 2.24 → −1.34, −0.45, 0.45, 1.34
Why we need this recap: AdaIN starts with exactly this step.
Unit 3 · 59 / 77
08 · StyleGAN · idea 2: AdaIN
AdaIN: wipe the style, add a new one
AdaIN(x, w) = γ × x_norm + β
AdaIN = Adaptive Instance Normalisation
1
Normalise x → x_norm. This strips the current style.
2
A small linear layer turns w into γ (scale) and β (shift).
3
Output = γ × x_norm + β. This adds the new style.
Worked: one value
x_norm = 1.34 (last slide), γ = 2, β = 0.5
γ × x_norm = 2 × 1.34 = 2.68
Output = 2.68 + 0.5 = 3.18
Why we need AdaIN: it is how w actually changes the image.
Unit 3 · 60 / 77
08 · StyleGAN · idea 2: where w goes
w enters at every layer
w (one vector)
4 × 4
own w → γ, β
8 × 8
own w → γ, β
16 × 16
own w → γ, β
32 × 32
own w → γ, β
64 × 64
own w → γ, β
128 × 128
own w → γ, β
The same w goes to every layer, small to large.
Each layer has its own linear layer w → (γ, β). So each layer reads different style information from w.
Why we need this: style can act at every scale, not just at the start.

Unit 3 · 63 / 77
08 · StyleGAN · mixing as training
Mixing during training
StyleGAN also mixes styles while it trains, on some batches.
1
Pick two random z vectors.
2
Map both: z_A → w_A, z_B → w_B.
3
Use w_A up to a random layer, then switch to w_B.
4
Each layer’s style must work with any other style. So styles stay independent: a regulariser.
Why we need mixing in training: it stops neighbouring layers relying on each other.

08 · StyleGAN · training trick (v1)
Grow the image step by step
4 × 4
8 × 8
16 × 16
…
1,024 × 1,024
phase 9
v1 kept ProGAN’s progressive growing: train small, then add layers.
blended = (1 − α) × old + α × new
α goes slowly from 0 (only old) to 1 (only new).
Worked: one pixel
α = 0.25, old pixel 0.8, new pixel 0.4
Old part: 0.75 × 0.8 = 0.6
New part: 0.25 × 0.4 = 0.1
Blended = 0.6 + 0.1 = 0.7
Why we need growing: each new size only has to add detail, not learn everything at once.
Unit 3 · 67 / 77
08 · StyleGAN · truncation
Truncation in W: ψ
w′ = w_mean + ψ × (w − w_mean)
w_mean = average w over 10,000 random z
Worked: one number
w_mean = 0.2, w = 1.0, ψ = 0.7
Gap: w − w_mean = 1.0 − 0.2 = 0.8
Shrink: 0.7 × 0.8 = 0.56
w′ = 0.2 + 0.56 = 0.76
ψ
result
1.0
full variety, some odd faces
0.7
high quality, good variety
0.5
very high quality, less variety
0
always the average face
Why we need ψ: one knob trades variety for quality. Recall Unit 2’s truncation in z.
Unit 3 · 68 / 77
08 · StyleGAN · truncation
Why truncate in W, not z
In z (Unit 2)
Re-sample values beyond a limit t.
z is entangled. Shrinking z changes features unevenly.
In W (StyleGAN)
Pull w toward w_mean by ψ.
W is closer to linear. Every style shrinks smoothly toward the average face.
Same trade in both: quality up, variety down. W gives the cleaner trade.
Why we need W for truncation: a smooth pull keeps faces natural as ψ shrinks.

08 · StyleGAN · impact
Why StyleGAN matters
1 · Mapping networks
Now standard: transform z before using it.
2 · Multi-scale style
Now standard: coarse, medium and fine control.
3 · Untangled latents
Now standard: directions mean features.
GAN inversion: find the w for a real photo, then edit it.
Trained on cars, rooms, cats and art, not just faces.
It proved GANs can be photo-real.
Why we need StyleGAN’s ideas: later models build on them, including in Unit 4.
Unit 3 · 72 / 77
08 · StyleGAN · check
Check: StyleGAN
1
Why a mapping network instead of z directly?
Z must fill a round shape, so features mix; W can follow the data, so features separate.
2
What are AdaIN’s two steps?
Normalise (wipe the old style), then γ × x_norm + β from w (add the new style).
3
w_A at coarse layers, w_B at fine layers: what image?
A’s face shape and pose with B’s colouring and texture.
4
Style (w) vs noise: what does each control?
w = what (“curly hair”); noise = exactly where (“where each curl falls”).
5
Why start from a learned constant, not z?
w and noise already reach every layer, so all variation comes from them.
Why it matters: these five answers are the whole StyleGAN generator.

IS = exp( E_x [ KL( p(y|x) ‖ p(y) ) ] )

AdaIN
γ × (x − mean) ÷ std + β, γ and β from w

w′ = w_mean + ψ × (w − w_mean)

(1 − α) × old + α × new

09 · Wrap-up · quiz · calculations
Work these out by hand
1
Every image is “class 1” with the same probabilities. What is IS?
p(y) = p(y|x) → KL = 0 → IS = exp(0) = 1
2
1-D FID: μ_r = 0, σ_r = 1, μ_f = 1, σ_f = 1?
Mean part (0 − 1)² = 1; spread part (1 − 1)² = 0 → FID = 1
3
AdaIN: x_norm = −0.45, γ = 2, β = 0.5?
2 × (−0.45) + 0.5 = −0.9 + 0.5 = −0.4
4
Truncation: ψ = 0.5, w_mean = 0, w = 2?
0 + 0.5 × (2 − 0) = 1
5
Overall FID 22.3; groups A 15.1, B 18.4, C 52.8. Is the GAN good for everyone?
No: group C (52.8) is far worse; the overall 22.3 hides it.
Why it matters: each answer uses one formula from the sheet.
